The PVM is concentrated on $\sigma(A)$, and a real $\lambda$ belongs to $\sigma(A)$ exactly when every neighborhood of $\lambda$ has nonzero spectral projection. For $z\notin\sigma(A)$, the bounded resolvent is the multiplier $(\lambda-z)^{-1}$, maps into exactly $D(A)$, and has norm at most $\operatorname{dist}(z,\sigma(A))^{-1}$ (with the zero-space convention $1/\infty=0$). The operators $U_A(t)=e^{itA}$ form a strongly continuous unitary group on all of $H$, with the exact derivative criterion $$\lim_{t\to0}\frac{U_A(t)x-x}{t}\text{ exists in }H\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in D(A),\qquad \left.\frac{d}{dt}U_A(t)x\right|_{t=0}=iAx.$$ They preserve $D(A)$ and its graph norm and commute with $A$ on that domain. The group with this exact generator is unique. PVMs, Borel calculus and groups transport under unitary intertwiners, and an isometry intertwining the groups for all real times has a reducing closed range and intertwines the PVMs. The construction uses countably generated subspaces attached to each finite tuple of vectors and their uniquely determined compatible calculus; it does not choose an arbitrary global cyclic decomposition or an orthonormal basis of $H$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$. - $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$. - $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values agree. - $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes that $T$ is closable. **Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition. 1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and $\overline T\subseteq T^*$. 2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$, the inclusion reversal of [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$ ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense domain $D(T)$.) 3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal, so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are equalities. 4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$ by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and $T$ a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$. Write $(z-T)x=zx-Tx$ for $x\in D(T)$. The **resolvent set** of $T$ is $$\rho(T):=\{z\in\mathbb C:\ z-T:D(T)\to H\text{ is bijective and }(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)\},$$ where $\mathcal B(H)$ is the space of bounded everywhere defined operators on $H$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]); the **spectrum** is $\sigma(T):=\mathbb C\setminus\rho(T)$. For $z\in\rho(T)$ the bounded operator $$R_T(z):=(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$$ is the **resolvent** of $T$ at $z$. This is the library convention used throughout the page, matching the bounded resolvent of [[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]: the shift is $zI-T$, with coefficient $-1$ on $T$. **The resolvent determines $T$ back.** If $z\in\rho(T)$ and $R:=R_T(z)$, then $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $TRy=zRy-y$ for $y\in H$; equivalently $T=zI-R^{-1}$ with $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$, and $R(z-T)x=x$ for $x\in D(T)$, $(z-T)Ry=y$ for $y\in H$. **Nonempty resolvent set forces closedness, without the closed graph theorem.** Assume $\rho(T)\ne\varnothing$ and fix $z\in\rho(T)$ with $R:=R_T(z)$. Choose a bound $C\ge0$ such that $\|Rv\|\le C\|v\|$. The map $F(v,w)=w-Rv$ is continuous, since $\|F(v,w)-F(v',w')\|\le\|w-w'\|+C\|v-v'\|$. Its zero set $\Gamma(R)=F^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed. Because $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $(z-T)Rv=v$ for every $v\in H$, the graph of $T$ is $$\Gamma(T)=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}=\{(Rv,zRv-v):v\in H\}=\Phi(\Gamma(R)),$$ where $\Phi(v,w):=(w,zw-v)$ is a continuous linear bijection of $H\oplus H$ with continuous inverse $\Psi(u,v)=(zu-v,u)$, since $\Phi(\Psi(u,v))=(u,z u-(zu-v))=(u,v)$ and $\Psi(\Phi(v,w))=\Psi(w,zw-v)=(v,w)$. A homeomorphism carries closed sets to closed sets, so $\Gamma(T)$ is closed and $T$ is closed. No closed graph theorem and hence no choice principle is used here. For the zero operator on a nonzero $H$, $\rho(0)=\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$: the nonzero shifts have inverse $z^{-1}I$, whereas the zero shift is not bijective. If $H=\{0\}$, every shift is the unique bijection of the zero space, so $\rho(T)=\mathbb C$ and $\sigma(T)=\varnothing$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a real constant $C \ge 0$ such that $$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$ Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The **operator norm** of $T$ is $$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$ The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]). In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice principle is used for this assertion. The same number is the least bound of $T$: $$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$ If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives $$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$ When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$, so $\|T\| = 0$.
Let $a\in\mathbb C$, $r>0$, and $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$. For every integer $m$, $$\int_\gamma(z-a)^m\,dz=\begin{cases}2\pi i,&m=-1,\\0,&m\ne-1.\end{cases}$$

Let $a\in\mathbb C$, let $R>0$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on the disc $$D(a,R)=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C:|\zeta-a|<R\}.$$ If $0<r<R$, $|z-a|<r$, and $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$, then $$f(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\,d\zeta.$$
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: [Gap and correctly ordered Neumann inverse] By [F1], the spectral support of $H_0$ is $\sigma(H_0)$. For $z\in\Gamma$, $|z-E|=g/2$ and every other spectral point $t$ has $|z-t|\ge|t-E|-|z-E|\ge g/2$. Thus $\|R_0(z)\|\le2/g$. The operator $H_\lambda$ is closed on $D$: if $x_n\to x$ and $H_\lambda x_n\to y$, then $H_0x_n\to y-\lambda Vx$, so closedness of $H_0$ gives $x\in D$ and $H_\lambda x=y$; the domain remains dense. On $D$, $z-H_\lambda=(I-\lambda VR_0(z))(z-H_0)$. Its first factor has the Neumann inverse [F2], since $\|\lambda VR_0(z)\|\le q_\lambda<1$. Therefore the displayed ordered series gives a two-sided inverse with range exactly $D$, and its geometric estimates give (a). Uniform convergence on the circle and each compact coupling subdisk proves norm holomorphy in $\lambda$; local inverse Neumann series give holomorphy in $z$ on the resolvent set. When $v=0$ this series is constant for all couplings. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

[Idempotence from two contours] Fix $\lambda\in\Omega_v$. Step 1.1 bounds the inverse uniformly on $\Gamma$, and another inverse Neumann series gives a resolvent annulus around it. Integrals of a holomorphic operator-valued function over concentric circles in that annulus are independent of radius: differentiating $\int_0^{2\pi}f(E+\rho e^{it})i\rho e^{it}\,dt$ in $\rho$ gives the integral of the periodic $t$ derivative of $f(E+\rho e^{it})e^{it}$, hence zero. Take an outer circle for $z$ and an inner circle for $w$. The inverse equations give $R_\lambda(z)R_\lambda(w)=[R_\lambda(w)-R_\lambda(z)]/(z-w)$, and also commutation of resolvents. In its double integral, the first term integrates in the outer variable to the inner projection integral because $\oint dz/(z-w)=2\pi i$; the second integrates in the inner variable to zero because $\oint dw/(z-w)=0$. Compact continuous integrals can be interchanged by norm Riemann sums. Annular independence identifies both circle integrals with $P_\lambda$, proving $P_\lambda^2=P_\lambda$. Resolvent commutation also gives $P_\lambda R_\lambda(z)=R_\lambda(z)P_\lambda$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]

[Graph domains, commutation and holomorphy] The identity $H_\lambda R_\lambda(z)=zR_\lambda(z)-I$ makes the contour integrand continuous into the complete graph space of the closed $H_\lambda$. Integrating there proves $P_\lambda H\subset D$ and $H_\lambda P_\lambda=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint_\Gamma zR_\lambda(z)\,dz=:C_\lambda\in\mathcal B(H)$. On $D$ the other inverse equation gives $R_\lambda(z)H_\lambda=zR_\lambda(z)-I$, so integration gives $P_\lambda H_\lambda=C_\lambda$ there. Thus the range and kernel reduce the operator with its domain. The uniform coupling series makes both $P_\lambda$ and $C_\lambda$ norm holomorphic. Since $H_0P_\lambda=C_\lambda-\lambda VP_\lambda$, the pair $(P_\lambda,H_0P_\lambda)$ is holomorphic into $\mathcal B(H,H\oplus H)$ and takes values in the closed graph of $H_0$; hence $P_\lambda$ is holomorphic as an operator into that graph space. In particular, the finite restriction $A_\lambda$ is well-defined on all of $M_\lambda$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, algebra]

[Initial projection and rank throughout the disk] At zero coupling [F1] evaluates the resolvent contour as the PVM projection on the real interior; its only unperturbed spectral point is $E$, so this is $P_0$. This evaluation follows by spectral pairings: scalar circle kernels integrate to one inside and zero outside [F3]; norm Riemann sums converge uniformly in the spectral variable, since the spectrum is at distance at least $g/2$ from the circle, allowing interchange with its finite scalar measures. The circle length $\pi g$ and step 1.1 give $\|P_\lambda-P_0\|\le q_\lambda/(1-q_\lambda)$. If bounded idempotents $P,Q$ have $\|P-Q\|<1$, then $x\in\operatorname{ran}P$ and $Qx=0$ imply $\|x\|=\|(P-Q)x\|<\|x\|$ unless $x=0$; therefore $Q|_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is injective, and the reverse restriction is also injective. For $s,t\in[0,1]$, the inverse equations give $R_{s\lambda}(z)-R_{t\lambda}(z)=(s-t)\lambda R_{s\lambda}(z)VR_{t\lambda}(z)$, hence $\|P_{s\lambda}-P_{t\lambda}\|\le q_\lambda|s-t|/(1-q_\lambda)^2$. Choose an integer $N>q_\lambda/(1-q_\lambda)^2$ and compare the finite path $P_{j\lambda/N}$, $0\le j\le N$. At each adjacent pair the two injections and finite dimension imply equal rank. Starting with rank $r$ proves rank $r$ at $\lambda$, even when the direct distance estimate is at least one. If $q_\lambda=0$ the path is constant. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F3, algebra]

[All spectral values of the finite restriction are inside] Put $M=M_\lambda$, $A=A_\lambda$, $P=P_\lambda$ and $Q=I-P$. For $z\in\Gamma$, resolvent commutation and the inverse equations give $R_\lambda(z)|_M=(z-A)^{-1}$ on $M$. If $Au=\alpha u$ with $u\ne0$, then $\alpha\notin\Gamma$ by those equations and $R_\lambda(z)u=(z-\alpha)^{-1}u$. The equation $Pu=u$ and its contour definition give winding number one for $\alpha$, so $\alpha\in\Delta$. In a finite basis of $M$, $w-A$ is invertible exactly when its kernel is zero [F3]; thus every spectral point of $A$ is an eigenvalue and lies in $\Delta$. There are at most $r$ distinct such points, since eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent: in a shortest nontrivial relation among them, applying $A-\alpha I$ for one term removes that term and leaves a shorter nontrivial relation. There is at least one: otherwise $(z-A)^{-1}$ is holomorphic throughout a neighborhood of the closed disk, and the scalar Cauchy formula [F3] makes its contour integral zero entrywise, contradicting its integral $I_M$ and $r\ge1$. Here the zero integral follows by applying the Cauchy formula to $(z-E)(z-A)^{-1}$ at $E$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, F3, algebra]

[Complementary inverse on its exact domain] For $w\in\Delta$ define $B(w)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint_\Gamma R_\lambda(z)/(z-w)\,dz$. As in step 3.1 its range lies in $D$. The identity $(w-H_\lambda)R_\lambda(z)=I-(z-w)R_\lambda(z)$ gives $(w-H_\lambda)B(w)=I-P$ on $H$; its right-hand counterpart gives $B(w)(w-H_\lambda)=I-P$ on $D$. Resolvent commutation shows $B(w)$ commutes with $P,Q$. The bounded map $B_Q(w)=QB(w)Q$ therefore maps $QH$ into $D\cap QH$ and satisfies both inverse equations for $w-H_\lambda$ on that exact complementary domain. No assertion that $B(w)P=0$ is needed. The idempotent splitting is $H=M\oplus QH$ and, since $P H\subset D$ and $P$ preserves $D$, its domain splitting is $D=M\oplus(D\cap QH)$. The complementary domain is dense in $QH$, since applying the bounded $Q$ to approximants from the dense $D$ preserves $D$ and approximates every vector of $QH$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, F3, construct, algebra]

[Exactly the interior spectrum and generalized eigenspaces] If $w\in\Delta\setminus\sigma(A)$, then the bounded operator $(w-A)^{-1}P+B_Q(w)$ maps $H$ into $D$ and is a two-sided inverse of $w-H_\lambda$ by the domain splitting and step 4.2. If $w\in\sigma(A)$, step 4.1 supplies a nonzero eigenvector in $M$, so $w\in\sigma(H_\lambda)$. This proves $\sigma(H_\lambda)\cap\Delta=\sigma(A)$, with its nonempty finite character from step 4.1. For such an eigenvalue $\alpha$ and an integer $k\ge1$, any generalized eigenvector $x\in D((H_\lambda-\alpha)^k)$ has $Qx$ in the complementary iterated domain, because $P,Q$ preserve $D$ and commute with $H_\lambda$. Step 4.2 makes $H_\lambda-\alpha$ injective on the complement; its powers are then injective on their domains, so $(H_\lambda-\alpha)^kQx=0$ forces $Qx=0$. Conversely $M\subset D$ is invariant, so every generalized eigenvector of $A$ is a generalized eigenvector of the full operator. This proves (c), including the exact complementary inverse. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, F2, algebra]

[Real coupling, zero branch and assembly] The bounded-perturbation adjoint identity is $D(H_\lambda^*)=D(H_0^*)=D$, $H_\lambda^*=H_0+\overline\lambda V$: subtract the everywhere-defined bounded term from the adjoint functional to identify exactly the domain of $H_0^*$. Thus $H_\lambda$ is self-adjoint for every real $\lambda$. For real $\lambda\in\Omega_v$, apply [F1] to this operator. Its spectrum misses the circle by step 1.1, so has positive distance from it by compactness of the circle and openness of the resolvent set. The same uniform scalar-kernel/Riemann-sum evaluation as in step 3.2 identifies $P_\lambda$ with the PVM on the real interior, hence an orthogonal spectral projection on the entire cluster. If $v=0$, the norm definition gives $V=0$, all resolvents and projections are constant for every complex coupling, and the exact PVM domain gives $H_0P_0=EP_0$; therefore the restriction is $E I$ and its spectrum is $\{E\}$. Steps 1.1–5.1 give the other assertions for arbitrary $H$ under CC, using only a finite path and finite bases; no individually ordered or holomorphic scalar branches have been introduced. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎
